usage: 의견 + 을 with 말하다, the default verb for voicing a view
의견 + 이 with 다르다, the set way to say 'we disagree'
의견 + 을 with 듣다, asking for input
의견 stands as a count noun you can put 다른 'other' in front of
examples: 제 의견은 조금 달라요.
My opinion is a little different.
Simple frame: 의견은 + adjective states where you stand on something.
이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 듣고 싶어요.
I'd like to hear your opinions on this issue.
Everyday frame: ~에 대해 (about) + 의견을 듣다, common in class or meetings.
회의에서 제 의견을 솔직하게 말했지만 받아들여지지 않았어요.
I gave my opinion frankly in the meeting, but it wasn't accepted.
Real situation: voicing 의견 at work, with the realistic outcome that it may be rejected.
nuance: 의견 is Sino-Korean (意見, 意 'mind/intention' + 見 'view/seeing'), literally 'how your mind sees something' — a considered position or judgment you can defend, usually about a topic, plan, or issue. The crucial contrast is with 생각: 생각 is the broad word for any 'thought' that crosses your mind, while 의견 is specifically a stance offered for discussion or evaluation, so a meeting asks for 의견 (positions), not just 생각 (musings). It is register-neutral and very common in school and workplace settings; the polite request 의견을 여쭤봐도 될까요? raises it a notch. Natural collocations: 의견을 말하다/내다/제시하다 (state/put forward), 의견이 다르다/같다 (disagree/agree), 의견을 모으다 (gather opinions), 반대 의견 (an opposing view). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 의견 every time you'd say 'I think' — 'I think it's good' is 좋은 것 같아요 or 좋다고 생각해요, NOT 좋은 의견이에요; 의견 is the opinion itself as a thing, not the act of thinking. Also don't say 의견하다 — there is no such verb; you 의견을 말하다.

Using 의견 where English 'I think...' just hedges — 'I think it'll rain' is 비가 올 것 같아요, not an 의견; 의견 is a stance offered for discussion.
Confusing 의견 with 생각 — 생각 is any thought; 의견 is a position on a topic, so a survey or meeting collects 의견, while daydreaming is 생각.

usage: 생각 + 이 with 나다, an idea or memory pops up by itself
생각 + 이 with 들다, a thought arises in you
생각 + 을 with 하다, the everyday 'to think things over'
생각 + 이다 evaluates a suggestion as good
examples: 좋은 생각이에요!
That's a good idea!
Simple frame: 생각 + 이에요 to praise a suggestion someone just made.
갑자기 어제 일이 생각났어요.
Yesterday's events suddenly came to mind.
Everyday frame: 생각나다 (one written verb) = 'to remember / cross one's mind' on its own.
며칠 동안 곰곰이 생각해 봤는데, 그냥 포기하는 게 나을 것 같아요.
I thought it over carefully for a few days, and I feel it's better to just give up.
Real situation: 생각해 보다 (think it over) leading to a tentative conclusion with ~것 같다.
nuance: 생각 is the native Korean catch-all noun for a 'thought', 'idea', or 'opinion' — anything that happens in the mind: memories, intentions, plans, beliefs, judgments. It is far broader and softer than Sino-Korean 의견 (a defined stance for discussion): 좋은 생각이에요 praises an idea, whereas 의견 frames it as a formal position. It also overlaps with 마음 ('heart/mind' as feeling/will), but 생각 is the cognitive 'thinking' side while 마음 is the emotional/volitional side — 생각이 바뀌다 = I changed my mind (reasoning), 마음이 바뀌다 = my heart changed (feelings). Register-neutral and one of the highest-frequency nouns in the language. Key collocations: 생각이 나다 (come to mind/remember), 생각이 들다 (a thought arises), 생각해 보다 (think it over), ~라고 생각하다 (to think that ~). The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb pattern: 'I think that it's true' is 사실이라고 생각해요 with the quotative ~라고, not 사실 생각해요; and 'I remember' is most naturally 생각나요, not a literal translation. Don't confuse 생각나다 (it comes to mind, intransitive) with 생각하다 (to actively think, transitive).

Using 생각 for a formal 'opinion' in a meeting where 의견 fits better — 생각 sounds casual/personal, 의견 sounds like a position offered for debate.

usage: 이유 + 이 with 있다, there exists a reason
이유 + 를 with 묻다, to inquire why
이유 + 없이 forms the adverb 'for no reason'
이유 + 로 with 무슨, asking the grounds 'on what reason'
examples: 특별한 이유는 없어요.
There's no special reason.
Simple frame: 이유 + 없다 to brush off a 'why' question politely.
늦은 이유를 설명해 주세요.
Please explain the reason you're late.
Everyday frame: [modifier]~(으)ㄴ + 이유 packs the reason into a noun phrase.
회사를 그만둔 이유는 여러 가지가 있지만, 가장 큰 이유는 건강이었어요.
There are several reasons I quit the company, but the biggest reason was my health.
Real situation: layering reasons (여러 가지 이유 / 가장 큰 이유) when explaining a big decision.
nuance: 이유 is Sino-Korean (理由, 理 'principle/logic' + 由 'cause/origin'), the 'reason' or grounds behind something — the answer to 'why?'. Its sharpest contrast is with 원인 (原因, 'cause'): 이유 is the justification or motive a person gives ('the reason I'm late'), often subjective and explainable, while 원인 is the objective, often impersonal cause of a result ('the cause of the fire', 화재의 원인). So you ask a friend 무슨 이유로 늦었어? but an investigator looks for the 원인 of an accident. Also distinguish 까닭, a more native, slightly literary synonym of 이유. Register-neutral and extremely common. Core collocations: 이유가 있다/없다, 이유를 묻다/대다/설명하다, 이유 없이 (for no reason), 그런 이유로 (for that reason), ~는 이유는 (the reason that ~ is). The English-speaker pitfall: don't bolt 이유 onto a 'because' clause redundantly — Korean already has 왜냐하면 ... 때문이에요 / ~기 때문에 to say 'because', so '왜냐하면 그 이유는...' is clunky; pick one. Also, 'the reason is because...' should be ~는 이유는 ... 때문이에요, where the sentence ends in 때문이다, not a second 이유.

usage: 관심 + 이 with 있다, the standard 'I'm interested'
관심 + 을 with 가지다, to develop interest
~에 marks the target; 관심이 많다 = lots of interest
관심 + 을 with 끌다, to draw interest
examples: 저는 한국 음악에 관심이 많아요.
I'm very interested in Korean music.
Simple frame: ~에 관심이 많다/있다 names the topic you're into with ~에.
요즘 사람들이 환경 문제에 관심을 가지기 시작했어요.
People have started taking an interest in environmental issues lately.
Everyday frame: 관심을 가지다 = to take/develop an interest, with 시작하다 for 'start to'.
처음엔 그냥 관심이었는데, 이제는 진지하게 공부하고 싶어졌어요.
At first it was just curiosity, but now I've come to want to study it seriously.
Real situation: 관심 as a starting spark that grows into a serious commitment.
nuance: 관심 is Sino-Korean (關心, 關 'to be connected/concerned' + 心 'heart/mind'), literally 'the heart being connected to something' — interest, concern, or attention directed at a topic, activity, or person. Two contrasts matter. Against 흥미 (興味): 흥미 is the felt 'fun/excitement' kind of interest, a momentary enjoyment (흥미로운 영화 = an interesting/fun movie), whereas 관심 is a steadier, often deliberate concern you choose to 'have' or 'give' (관심을 가지다). Against 호기심 (好奇心, curiosity): 호기심 is the itch to find out, while 관심 is broader attention or care. Note 관심 also means romantic/personal attention — 관심 있어? can imply 'do you like me?' in the right context. Register-neutral, very high frequency. Collocations: ~에 관심이 있다/없다/많다, 관심을 가지다/두다/끌다/받다, 관심 분야 (field of interest), 무관심 (indifference). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: the thing you're interested in takes ~에 (or ~에 대해), so it's 음악에 관심이 있어요, NOT 음악을 관심이 있어요 or 음악 관심 있어요. Also 'I'm interested' is a state with 있다 (관심이 있다), not 관심하다 — there is no verb 관심하다.

Swapping 관심 and 흥미 — a fun, momentary 'that's interesting!' is 흥미롭다, while 관심 is steady concern/attention you give to a topic or person.

usage: 하다 contracts to 해요, never 복잡하요
to have a lot on one's mind
머리가 복잡하다, an idiom for a cluttered, stressed mind
복잡하다 also covers crowded, tangled places
examples: 이 문제는 너무 복잡해요.
This problem is too complicated.
Simple frame: subject + 복잡해요 to call something hard to untangle.
주말이라서 시내가 사람들로 복잡했어요.
Because it was the weekend, downtown was crowded with people.
Everyday frame: 복잡하다 = 'crowded/congested' for places, with ~로 'with (people)'.
설명을 들을수록 더 복잡해져서, 결국 포기하고 싶어졌어요.
The more I listened to the explanation, the more complicated it got, so in the end I felt like giving up.
Real situation: 복잡해지다 (become complicated) showing a situation worsening as it's explained.
nuance: 복잡하다 is a Sino-Korean 하다-adjective (複雜 + 하다, 複 'multiple/layered' + 雜 'mixed/miscellaneous'), literally 'many things mixed together', so it spans three English ideas at once: (1) complicated/intricate (복잡한 문제 = a complex problem), (2) crowded/congested (길이 복잡하다 = the road is jammed), and (3) mentally cluttered/troubled (머리가 복잡하다 = my head is a mess). Its opposite is 간단하다 (simple). Contrast it with 어렵다: 어렵다 is 'difficult' (hard to do or understand, possibly even if simple in structure), while 복잡하다 stresses having too many tangled parts — a problem can be 복잡하지만 어렵지 않다 (complicated but not hard). As a 하다-adjective it conjugates 복잡해 → 복잡해요 (never 복잡하요), modifier 복잡한, adverb 복잡하게, and 'become complicated' is 복잡해지다. Register-neutral. The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 복잡하다 for a task that is merely 'hard' — use 어렵다 for difficulty; and for a crowded café, Koreans naturally say 사람이 많다 or 복잡하다, but never the literal 'busy'. Also avoid 복잡하고 있다 — it's a state (복잡해요), not an ongoing action.

Treating it as an action verb: 'I am being busy/complicated' is not 복잡하고 있어요; the state is simply 복잡해요 or 머리가 복잡해요.

usage: 맛 + 이 + 있다 fuses into the one word 맛있다
맛 + 이 + 없다 fuses into 맛없다
맛 + 을 with 보다, to sample the flavor
맛 as a count noun: which flavor/taste
examples: 이 국 맛이 어때요?
How does this soup taste?
Simple frame: 맛이 어때요? is the standard way to ask 'how does it taste?'
저는 단맛보다 매운맛을 더 좋아해요.
I like spicy flavor more than sweet flavor.
Everyday frame: flavor compounds 단맛(sweet)/매운맛(spicy)/짠맛(salty) + ~보다 to compare.
오랫동안 끓였더니 국물에서 깊은 맛이 나기 시작했어요.
After simmering it a long time, a deep flavor began to come out of the broth.
Real situation: 맛이 나다 (a flavor comes out) plus 깊은 맛 (deep, rich flavor) in cooking.
nuance: 맛 is the native Korean noun for taste or flavor — both the literal taste on the tongue and, by extension, the 'flavor/charm' of an experience (사는 맛 = the joy of living; 그 영화는 보는 맛이 있다 = that movie is fun to watch). Its most important behavior is fusion: 맛 + 있다 → 맛있다 (delicious) and 맛 + 없다 → 맛없다 (not tasty) are written as single words and are the everyday way to praise or pan food. Contrast 맛 with 향 (香, scent/aroma, from the nose, e.g. 커피 향) and with 식감 (食感, texture/mouthfeel) — Koreans separate flavor (맛), smell (향), and texture (식감). The five basic tastes form compounds: 단맛, 짠맛, 신맛(sour), 쓴맛(bitter), 매운맛(spicy/hot). Register-neutral, extremely high frequency. Collocations: 맛이 있다/없다, 맛을 보다 (taste it), 맛이 나다 (a taste comes out), 맛이 진하다/연하다 (strong/mild), 입맛 (appetite/palate). The English-speaker pitfall: 'this is tasty' is 맛있어요 (one word), not 맛이 좋아요 in casual speech (though 맛이 좋다 exists, it sounds more written/evaluative); and don't say 맛이 나빠요 for 'it tastes bad' — say 맛없어요. To ask 'what does it taste like?', use 무슨 맛이에요? or 맛이 어때요?, not a literal 'how is the taste'.

usage: 방법 + 이 with 있다, a way exists
방법 + 을 with 찾다, to look for a solution
adjective + 방법, naming a good approach
examples: 다른 방법이 없어요.
There's no other way.
Simple frame: 방법이 없다 = there's no method/option, a common resigned phrase.
이 단어를 외우는 좋은 방법이 있어요?
Is there a good way to memorize this word?
Everyday frame: [verb]~는 + 방법 = 'a way to do X', the go-to question for tips.
여러 방법을 다 시도해 봤지만, 결국 가장 단순한 방법이 제일 효과적이었어요.
I tried all sorts of methods, but in the end the simplest method was the most effective.
Real situation: surveying 여러 방법 (various methods) and concluding which worked best.
nuance: 방법 is Sino-Korean (方法, 方 'direction/manner' + 法 'rule/method'), the 'way', 'method', or 'means' of doing something — the procedure or approach to reach a goal. Compare it with 방식 (方式, 'style/mode/manner'): 방법 is the concrete how-to ('a method to fix it'), while 방식 is the overall style or fashion in which something is done (생활 방식 = lifestyle, 사고방식 = way of thinking) — you wouldn't say 사고방법. Also distinguish 수단 (手段, 'means/instrument', often the tool or even an unscrupulous means: 교통수단 = means of transport, 수단과 방법을 가리지 않다 = by any means necessary). Register-neutral, very common. Core collocations: 방법이 있다/없다, 방법을 찾다/알다/모르다/바꾸다, [동사]~는 방법 (a way to do ~), 해결 방법 (solution), 사용 방법 (how to use). The English-speaker pitfall is the 'a way to do X' frame: it's [verb in ~는 form] + 방법, e.g. 'a way to study' is 공부하는 방법, NOT 공부 방법 in spoken contexts (though 공부 방법 as a fixed noun-noun compound is fine for 'study method'). Don't say 방법으로 어떻게 when you just mean 어떻게 ('how') — 방법 is the noun 'method', not the question word 'how'.

usage: 장점 + 이 with 있다, an advantage exists
장점 + 이 with 많다, lots of good points
가장 큰 + 장점, ranking the top merit
to make the most of a strength
장점 + 을 with 살리다, to leverage an advantage
examples: 이 방법은 장점이 많아요.
This method has many advantages.
Simple frame: subject + 장점이 많다/있다 to list what's good about something.
온라인 수업의 장점은 시간을 아낄 수 있다는 거예요.
The advantage of online classes is that you can save time.
Everyday frame: ~의 장점은 ...라는 것이다, the set 'the advantage of X is that ~' pattern.
면접에서 자신의 장점과 단점을 솔직하게 말하는 게 좋아요.
In an interview, it's good to honestly state your own strengths and weaknesses.
Real situation: 장점과 단점 paired in the classic interview question about yourself.
nuance: 장점 is Sino-Korean (長點, 長 'long/superior' + 點 'point'), literally a 'strong point' — a merit, advantage, or strength of a thing, plan, or person. It is almost always used in deliberate contrast with its antonym 단점 (短點, 'short point' = weakness/drawback); the pair 장점과 단점 is a fixed collocation, like English 'pros and cons'. Compare 장점 with 강점 (強點, 'strong point/forte'): 강점 emphasizes a competitive strength relative to others (우리 회사의 강점 = our company's competitive edge), while 장점 is the neutral 'good point' of anything. Also note 좋은 점 (a more colloquial 'the good thing about it'). Register-neutral and common in reviews, interviews, and comparisons. Collocations: 장점이 있다/많다, 장점을 살리다 (leverage), 장점을 살펴보다 (examine the merits), 큰 장점, 최대 장점 (greatest advantage). The English-speaker pitfall: don't translate 'advantage' as 이득 or 이점 indiscriminately — 이득 (利得) is material 'gain/profit', and 이점 (利點) is 'an advantageous point/benefit' often in a strategic sense; for the everyday 'good point of X', 장점 is the natural choice. Also, when describing a person's virtue, 장점 (good trait) differs from 매력 (charm/appeal) — a reliable friend has a 장점, a charismatic one has 매력.

Using 이득 for 'advantage' of a method — 이득 is monetary gain; the merit/strength of a plan is its 장점.
Saying 장점이 좋다 — that's redundant ('the good point is good'); just say 장점이 있다/많다, or 좋은 점이 있다.

usage: 단점 + 이 with 있다, a weak point exists
단점 + 을 with 고치다, to improve a flaw
가장 큰 + 단점, ranking the worst weakness
to make up for a weakness
단점 + 을 with 보완하다, to compensate for a flaw
examples: 이 휴대폰은 단점이 거의 없어요.
This phone has almost no drawbacks.
Simple frame: subject + 단점이 없다/있다 to evaluate the downsides of a product.
제 단점은 가끔 너무 솔직하다는 거예요.
My weakness is that I'm sometimes too honest.
Everyday frame: ~의 단점은 ...라는 것이다, the 'my weakness is that ~' interview pattern.
이 방법의 단점은 시간이 오래 걸린다는 점인데, 그래도 가장 안전해요.
The drawback of this method is that it takes a long time, but it's still the safest.
Real situation: conceding a 단점 (~다는 점) while still recommending the option.
nuance: 단점 is Sino-Korean (短點, 短 'short/lacking' + 點 'point'), literally a 'short point' — a weakness, drawback, flaw, or shortcoming of a thing, plan, or person. It is the fixed antonym of 장점 (長點, merit), and the pair 장점과 단점 functions exactly like English 'pros and cons / strengths and weaknesses'. The key contrast to master is 단점 vs 약점 (弱點, 'weak point/vulnerability'): 단점 is a general flaw or downside that's just part of something (이 차의 단점 = this car's drawback, e.g. poor mileage), while 약점 is an exploitable vulnerability or sensitive spot — a rival attacks your 약점, a coach targets the opponent's 약점, and a personal sore subject is a 약점, not a 단점. Also compare 결점 (缺點, a 'defect/fault', slightly stronger, hints at something missing) and 흠 (a native word for a 'flaw/blemish'). Register-neutral. And don't say 단점이 나쁘다 ('the drawback is bad') — that's redundant; just 단점이 있다.

usage: 차이 + 이 with 있다, a difference exists
차이 + 이 with 나다, a difference appears between things
차이 + 이 with 크다, a large gap
~와 marks the thing compared against; 차이가 있다
examples: 두 사진은 차이가 거의 없어요.
The two photos have almost no difference.
Simple frame: A는/두 N은 + 차이가 없다/있다 to say things are (not) different.
이 두 단어는 의미에 큰 차이가 있어요.
These two words have a big difference in meaning.
Everyday frame: ~에 차이가 있다 (a difference IN ~), here 의미에 (in meaning).
가격은 비슷한데 품질에서 차이가 많이 나서, 결국 더 비싼 걸 샀어요.
The prices are similar, but there's a big difference in quality, so in the end I bought the more expensive one.
Real situation: 차이가 나다 in 품질에서 (in quality) driving a purchase decision.
nuance: 차이 is Sino-Korean (差異, 差 'discrepancy/gap' + 異 'different'), the 'difference', 'gap', or 'disparity' between two or more things. It pairs with two key verbs: 차이가 있다 (a difference exists, more static) and 차이가 나다 (a difference shows up/emerges, more dynamic, often for a noticeable gap, e.g. 실력 차이가 나다 = a clear skill gap). The thing you compare with takes ~와/과 (A는 B와 차이가 있다), and the dimension of difference takes ~에(서) (의미에 차이가 있다 = a difference in meaning). Contrast 차이 with 다르다, the adjective 'to be different': 다르다 describes that two things are not the same (A와 B는 달라요), while 차이 is the noun naming the gap itself (A와 B는 차이가 있어요) — Koreans often use 다르다 for a qualitative 'different' and 차이 for a measurable/quantifiable gap (나이 차이 = age gap, 온도 차이 = temperature difference). Don't confuse 차이 with 차별 (差別, 'discrimination'), which is unfair treatment based on a difference. Register-neutral, very common. Collocations: 차이가 있다/없다/나다/크다, 차이를 느끼다 (feel a difference), 큰 차이, 별 차이 없다 (no real difference), 나이 차이/시차 (time difference). The English-speaker pitfall: 'A is different from B' is most naturally A는 B와 달라요 (using 다르다 + 와), not A는 B에서 차이예요; reach for the noun 차이 when you mean 'the difference between/in', and the verb 다르다 when you simply mean 'differs'.

usage: 태도 + 이 with 좋다, a good manner/disposition
태도 + 이 with 나쁘다, a poor attitude
태도 + 를 with 바꾸다, to shift one's stance/manner
examples: 그 사람은 태도가 정말 좋아요.
That person has a really good attitude.
Simple frame: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다 to judge someone's manner or disposition.
선생님은 항상 학생들에게 친절한 태도로 말해요.
The teacher always speaks to students with a kind attitude.
Everyday frame: ~한 태도로 (with a ~ attitude) describes the manner of an action.
실력도 중요하지만, 일을 대하는 성실한 태도가 더 중요하다고 생각해요.
Skill matters too, but I think a sincere attitude toward work is more important.
Real situation: weighing 태도 (work attitude) against 실력 (skill) in a values statement.
nuance: 태도 is Sino-Korean (態度, 態 'form/manner/bearing' + 度 'degree/measure'), a person's 'attitude', 'manner', 'bearing', or 'stance' — both the outward way they carry and conduct themselves (공손한 태도 = a polite manner) and their inner posture toward something (인생을 대하는 태도 = one's attitude toward life). Contrast it with 자세 (姿勢): 자세 literally means physical 'posture/pose' (바른 자세로 앉다 = sit with good posture) but is also used figuratively for a committed 'attitude/stance', often a praiseworthy, proactive one (배우려는 자세 = a willing-to-learn attitude) — so 자세 leans toward earnest mindset, while 태도 is the broader, more neutral 'manner' that can be good OR bad (태도가 나쁘다 is normal; 자세가 나쁘다 usually means literal bad posture). Also distinguish 입장 (立場, 'position/standpoint' on an issue) and 성격 (性格, 'personality', a stable trait vs. a situational 태도). Register-neutral, common in evaluations of behavior, work, and manners. Collocations: 태도가 좋다/나쁘다, 태도를 바꾸다/취하다 (change/take an attitude), ~에 대한 태도 (attitude toward ~), 근무 태도 (work attitude), 강경한 태도 (a hard-line stance). The English-speaker pitfall: 'attitude' in English can imply a personality trait or even sass, but Korean 태도 is more about manner/conduct in a given context; for a fixed personality trait use 성격, and don't say 태도하다 — there is no such verb; you 태도를 취하다/보이다 (take/show an attitude).

usage: 느낌 + 이 with 좋다, something feels right
느낌 + 이 with 들다, an impression arises
느낌 + 이 with 오다, intuition kicks in
examples: 이 카페는 느낌이 좋아요.
This café has a good vibe.
Simple frame: 느낌이 좋다 to say a place/person gives a pleasant impression.
뭔가 잘못된 느낌이 들어요.
I get the feeling something is wrong.
Everyday frame: [modifier]~ㄴ + 느낌이 들다 = 'I get a ~ feeling/sense that ~'.
설명을 들어도 완전히 이해한 느낌이 안 와서, 한 번 더 물어봤어요.
Even after hearing the explanation, I didn't get the feeling I fully understood, so I asked once more.
Real situation: 느낌이 안 오다 (it doesn't click) prompting a follow-up question.
nuance: 느낌 is the native Korean noun from the verb 느끼다 ('to feel'), meaning a 'feeling', 'impression', 'sense', or 'vibe' — the subjective sensation or intuition something gives you, whether physical (차가운 느낌 = a cold feeling) or atmospheric (느낌이 좋은 사람 = someone who gives off a good vibe). The crucial contrast is with 기분 (氣分): 기분 is your own emotional 'mood/spirits' caused by events (기분이 좋다 = I'm in a good mood, 기분 나빠 = I'm upset), whereas 느낌 is the impression/sense you get OF something external (그 사람 느낌이 좋다 = that person gives a good impression — about them, not your mood). Also distinguish 감정 (感情, 'emotion' as a category: love, anger) and 감각 (感覺, 'sense/sensation', the faculty). Register-neutral and hugely frequent in casual speech, where 느낌 also works as a vague 'kind of, sort of, like' filler (약간 매운 느낌? = kind of spicy?). Collocations: 느낌이 좋다/이상하다, 느낌이 들다 (a feeling arises), 느낌이 오다 (it clicks/I get a hunch), 첫 느낌 (first impression), ~는 느낌 (a feeling of ~ing). The English-speaker pitfall: don't use 느낌 for your own mood — 'I feel good/happy today' is 오늘 기분이 좋아요, NOT 느낌이 좋아요 (which describes an external thing's vibe). mistakes: Using 느낌 for your own mood: 'I'm in a good mood' is 기분이 좋아요, while 느낌이 좋아요 means 'it/he gives a good vibe' (an external impression).
Saying 느낌하다 — there's no verb; the natural patterns are 느낌이 들다 / 느낌이 오다, or the source verb 느끼다 ('느꼈어요').
Forgetting the ~ㄴ/는 modifier: 'a warm feeling' is 따뜻한 느낌, and 'I get the feeling it's true' is 사실인 느낌이 들어요, not 사실 느낌.
